findings.assertion: After floods in 1604 and 1607, elite flood-control policy shifted toward moving water out of the closed basin rather than relying only on retention/containment; Candiani frames this as a decision about whose property and labor the project protected.
findings.limitations: Full chapter, expenditure records and Indigenous testimony not examined; avoid treating abstract as proof of every implementation detail.

findings.assertion: The Huehuetoca drainage scheme involved a channel and tunnel associated with Enrico Martínez and intensive Indigenous corvée/repartimiento labor; Candiani's abstract gives an approximate 60,000 mobilized workers, a figure needing examination of its source and counting method.
findings.limitations: 60,000 is the author's estimate in an abstract, not an independently checked person-count; do not frame as unique annual laborers.

findings.assertion: The flood beginning in 1629 left much of Mexico City inundated in varying degrees until the 1634 dry season; the flood was a prolonged urban emergency, not one single 40-hour rainfall event whose water immediately receded.
findings.source_locator: García Martínez, Arqueología Mexicana 68, online excerpt of pp.50–57
findings.limitations: Exact flood onset, rainfall duration and water heights need primary meteorological/municipal record crosscheck; printed full article unavailable.

findings.assertion: The flood produced differentiated suffering: García Martínez specifically reports collapse of poorer adobe housing, severe deprivation, and potentially tens of thousands of deaths and departures; his figures are explicitly uncertain rather than census totals.
findings.source_locator: García Martínez web excerpt, paragraphs on adobe houses, deaths, approximate city population and migration
findings.limitations: Estimated 30,000 deaths, 50,000 emigrants and 150,000 residents must not be published as exact measured totals.

findings.assertion: Responses to the 1629 flood were also contests over authority and religious patronage: religious corporations proposed competing saints and Marian images as intercessors, alongside practical environmental explanations and hydraulic proposals.
findings.source_locator: Cuéllar Meléndez 2017 abstract lines 49–53; Hoberman 1974 article extract
findings.limitations: Which image was promoted by each group, their dates/processions and municipal decisions require full text and primary records.

findings.assertion: The present Templo de la Profesa should not be read as an untouched sixteenth-century Jesuit building: INAH records a 1597 construction start and a major rebuilding in 1714 in response to damage from the 1629 inundation, directed by Pedro de Arrieta.
geographies: Calle Madero / Templo de la Profesa
findings.source_locator: INAH Lugares direct monument entry lines 19–23
findings.limitations: Exact surviving original fabric, restoration chronology and 2026 building access are unverified; do not label specific visible stones 1597.

findings.assertion: García Martínez singles out the Santa Catarina and Santa Ana neighborhoods as still largely deserted after the 1634 drying period; this provides a geographically situated counterpoint to narratives focused only on viceregal central squares.
findings.source_locator: Arqueología Mexicana 68 web excerpt: Santa Catarina and Santa Ana paragraph
findings.limitations: Historical barrio boundaries, modern place equivalents and individual surviving structures have not been verified.

findings.assertion: A visitor at the historic core should understand that the early seventeenth-century city occupied a rapidly changing lake-edge environment: López's MIT dissertation abstract contrasts the island city of 1521, a lake-margin city around 1629, and reclaimed land by 1700.
findings.limitations: These are interpretive period descriptions, not survey-grade georeferenced shorelines; no field map overlay is currently licensed or verified.

findings.assertion: Huehuetoca and the drainage corridor northwest of the capital are integral to understanding the 1629 flood even though they are not an immediate downtown walk stop; claims about the visible present-day trench require a separate site and engineering-history audit.
findings.source_locator: Candiani chapter abstract; INAH Anales 1887 historical report catalog pp.167–193
findings.limitations: The 1636 report is identified bibliographically, not read; no present-day accessible trace or walking route authenticated.

findings.assertion: The flood-control question was contested rather than technologically inevitable: an INAH scholarly abstract reports that Dutch engineer Adrian Boot, arriving in 1614, opposed Martínez's drainage proposal and favored renewed regulation of lake waters.
findings.source_locator: López 2017 INAH article abstract; Candiani 2014 chapter 2 abstract
findings.limitations: Original Boot/Martínez reports and full specialist articles unexamined; the comparison cannot yet specify dimensions or outcomes of rival designs.

findings.assertion: The reported 1630 Acolman dam belongs to a different, northeast-basin water-management locality from the capital's northwestern Huehuetoca outlet. Treat the regional network and chronology as separate interventions rather than drawing one unverified continuous downtown-to-Acolman construction project.
findings.source_locator: Skopyk & Martínez Yrízar 2017 indexed abstract; Candiani chapter abstract
findings.limitations: Acolman paper, archival maps and field observations not read; no verified combined alignment available.
